topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Workforce wellbeing and enablement

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider cared about and promoted the wellbeing of their staff.

Staff told us they felt supported by leaders, who cared about their welfare and would encourage them to develop professionally including those who aspired to be leaders themselves in the future. One staff member told us “I feel very supported. The provider supported me through my education, and now to do training courses that I have requested to develop my skills. I am happy here”.

All staff received regular opportunities meet with managers, which always started with a discussion about their own welfare, and any factors in their personal life which they could be supported with support their wellbeing and their ability to work. When new staff joined the service, they told us this was a positive process which gave them opportunity shadow other staff and learn the needs of people before they started working with them. One member of staff told inspectors “I enjoy working with the people here and I have no concern. When I joined, I got lots of support and the induction was really good”.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Effective
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Effective – this means we looked for evidence that people’s care, treatment and support achieved good outcomes and promoted a good quality of life, based on best available evidence.

At our last assessment we rated this key question Requires Improvement. At this assessment the rating has remained Requires Improvement. This meant the effectiveness of people’s care, treatment and support did not always achieve good outcomes or was inconsistent.
keyQuestionRatings.narrative: This service is not always effective

topicareas.name: Assessing needs

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always make sure people’s care and treatment were effective because they did not always check and discuss people’s health, care, wellbeing and communication needs with them.

Although people’s needs were assessed, the level of guidance in place did not provide a consistent or clear plan of the care they should receive. The service were supporting people living with complex and enduring mental health conditions, however guidance primarily referred to medication and input from health professionals to manage this, rather than any actions staff could do proactively to promote their emotional wellbeing.

The quality of information in people’s care planning had improved since the last inspection and the provider had recently switched to digital records, but it was still not always clear that these were up to date or reflective of current needs. For example, one person was recorded as not liking meat but their care notes showed them eating this most days indicating that this was not the case.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Consent to care and treatment

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider told people about their rights around consent and respected these when delivering person-centred care and treatment.

We observed that staff sought consent before performing any care tasks, which was clearly recorded within people’s daily care notes as well being seen in practice during our inspection. Staff were trained and knowledgeable about the principles of consent, and the rights of people to make their own choices. Where people were assessed as lacking mental capacity to make decisions, a best interest meeting was held with people’s representatives to make decisions on their behalf to ensure their welfare.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Delivering evidence-based care and treatment

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not plan and deliver people’s care and treatment with them, including what was important and mattered to them.

The model of care at The Chestnuts did not reflect best practice for a service supporting individuals with complex mental health needs. Guidance in place remained inconsistent about how people’s welfare could be promoted, and there was limited evidence that people had regular opportunities to discuss their wellbeing with staff or that this was proactively offered. The service had not considered wider factors such as promoting independence, meaningful social activity and person-centred goals that could promote people’s mental health, alongside any medical support or medication they received to manage this.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: How staff, teams and services work together

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always work well across teams and services to support people.

We observed that staff treated people with kindness and were generally knowledgeable about how to keep them safe and support their physical health needs. However, there were significant inconsistencies in staff understanding around people’s goals and aspirations, and there was little evidence of staff working collaboratively to support people in achieving them or to improve their independence.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Monitoring and improving outcomes

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always routinely monitor people’s care and treatment to continuously improve it. They did not always ensure that outcomes were positive and consistent, or that they met both clinical expectations and the expectations of people themselves.

Although people’s physical health outcomes were largely monitored well, there was a lack of consistent monitoring of people’s wider social outcomes and what they wanted to achieve from their time at The Chestnuts. There was a lack of detailed plans of how people would be supported to achieve any goals or aspirations, and no evidence that these were being reviewed alongside people and adjusted accordingly. Keyworker meetings were taking place but the records of these were largely identical from month to month or did not reflect a detailed discussion with each person about their care.

However, where people were at risk through malnutrition or dehydration staff were ensuring that people’s food and drink intake were being monitored, as well as their weight regularly checked. For people who had conditions such as diabetes we saw their blood sugar levels were being monitored regularly, to allow staff to intervene if these were to become unsafe.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Supporting people to live healthier lives

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider supported people to manage their health and wellbeing to maximise their independence, choice and control. Staff supported people to live healthier lives and where possible, reduce their future needs for care and support.

People were able to access a range of health services both within and outside of the home. This included visits from services such as opticians and chiropodists on a regular basis, as well as attending appointments with the GP or mental health services which staff supported people to attend. Where people were less comfortable with leaving the building to attend appointments, staff had worked with people to improve their confidence. We identified one person had been reluctant to leave the building, however staff would now ensure they made them aware of the appointment well in advance to provide them with reassurance and they were now attending these in person which was a major step for them. One person told us “I went out this morning to have a blood test. Staff went with me”.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Responsive
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Responsive – this means we looked for evidence that the provider met people’s needs.

At our last assessment we rated this key question Requires Improvement. At this assessment the rating has remained Requires Improvement. This meant people’s needs were not always met.

The service was in breach of legal regulation in relation to person-centred care
keyQuestionRatings.narrative: This service is not always responsive

topicareas.name: Care provision, Integration and continuity

evidenceCategory.commentary:
There were some shortfalls in how the provider understood the diverse health and care needs of people and their local communities, so care was not always joined-up, flexible or supportive of choice and continuity.

People were supported by a consistent staff team, who were kind and knowledgeable about their health needs. However, they did not all have the same understanding of what people wanted to achieve from living at The Chestnuts, or a coherent plan to help them to achieve these goals. People came from diverse backgrounds and cultures, however these were not always clearly reflected in their care or understood by leaders and staff.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Equity in access

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always made sure that people could access the care, support and treatment they needed when they needed it.

People were not able to access regular person-centred engagement, activity or support that was tailored to them to allow them like empowered lives focused on their skills and abilities. However, people were able to access health support when required. For people who might be reluctant or less able to leave the home, this included access home visits from health care professionals whilst those who could attend in person were supported by staff to do so. If people’s health and care needs deteriorated, this was responded to appropriately, so people received the support they needed.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Equity in experiences and outcomes

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Staff and leaders did not always actively listen to information about people who are most likely to experience inequality in experience or outcomes. This meant people’s care was not always tailored in response to this.

The provider had not fully considered barriers faced by people with a mental health diagnosis in wider society, and how people could be supported to overcome these. For instance, people had goals around living independently, getting paid or voluntary employment or forming a relationship but there was no clear plan of how this would be achieved. We saw some consideration had been given to how people from diverse cultures could be supported to access care that promoted their culture and heritage, but again this had not been fully considered or demonstrated in practice.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Listening to and involving people

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always make it easy for people to share feedback and ideas, or raise complaints about their care, treatment and support. Staff did not always involve people in decisions about their care or tell them what had changed as a result.

Opportunities were not always taken to involve people in their own care, to ensure it continued to be shaped around the wishes and preferences. Although there were service user meetings which were well attended and discussed matters such as activities and food, these were not taking place frequently. There had only been 3 meetings between March 2026 and the date of our inspection, and 1 of these had been a very brief meeting to discuss the location of the summer trip. People had monthly keyworker meetings, however the records from these were largely identical each month and were primarily written about people rather than with them. There was also no clear evidence that people had been involved in writing their own care plan.

The provider did undertake annual surveys to gather the feedback of people, relatives and professionals who worked with the home. This feedback was mostly positive and where areas for improvement were identified, these were implemented in practice. All those we spoke with told us that any concerns they raised would be listen to by leaders, although there had been few complaints within the last year. One person told us “I could speak to (Manager name). She is nice”.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Person-centred Care

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always make sure people were at the centre of their care and treatment choices and they did not always work in partnership with people, to decide how to respond to any relevant changes in people’s needs.

We saw some examples of person-centred care being undertaken, however there were further opportunities missed to ensure the care people received fully reflected them as an individual. For example, one person had a religious faith and were being supported to attend their place of worship regularly. However, there was no written guidance to help staff who were unfamiliar with their faith understand what it meant to them, or how they wished to be supported. We identified that certain staff had refused to enter their place of worship with them because of their own religion, which the provider hadn’t fully explored with staff as to why they might be uncomfortable doing. There was no reference to if they wanted to be supported to attend local religious festivals, and we noted they were largely eating the same food as their peers despite it being recorded they would like more food from their culture.

Likewise, another person was from a different culture and was supported to have their hair cut in a specialist hairdressers to reflect their heritage. However, there was no other guidance on their culture and how they may wish to express this, or consideration of how they could be supported to participate in their own community.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Planning for the future

evidenceCategory.commentary:
People were not supported to plan for important life changes, so they could have enough time to make informed decisions about their future, including at the end of their life.

There was no consistent or personalised plan setting out how staff should work with people to support them to achieve any future goals, such as living independently once more. There were multiple people who were described in their care plans as having aspirations to live in their own home in the future, however there was no detailed plan setting out how the service would work with them to equip them with the skills to do so. The majority of staff we spoke with stated there was either nobody who could live independently, or gave us the names of other service users where their care plan did not contain any references to independent living. One staff member told us “Everybody is fine here. Nobody has a goal to live by themselves”. Some people living at the service were in romantic relationships, however there was no guidance of any sort to describe how they may wish to be supported to maintain or develop these relationships or to ensure they were safe for both partners.

However we identified people had been supported to put in place end of life care plans in case their health were to deteriorate, which included references to spiritual or religious wishes and people they would like to be involved on their behalf.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Providing Information

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider supplied appropriate, accurate and up-to-date information in formats that were tailored to individual needs.

We saw information was provided in easy read formats where required including activities timetables, minutes of meetings and copies of their keyworker reports to ensure people were able to process information in a way that was personalised to them. Staff communicated patiently with people, and would repeat things if needed and give people time to respond to ensure they had time to process information and make decisions for themselves.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Safe
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Safe – this means we looked for evidence that people were protected from abuse and avoidable harm. At our last assessment we rated this key question Inadequate. At this assessment the rating has changed to Requires Improvement. This meant some aspects of the service were not always safe and there was limited assurance about safety. There was an increased risk that people could be harmed.

The service was in breach of legal regulation in relation to safe and care treatment
keyQuestionRatings.narrative: This service is not always safe

topicareas.name: Infection prevention and control

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always assess or manage the risk of infection. They did not always detect and control the risk of it spreading or share concerns with appropriate agencies promptly.

Although cleanliness had improved since our last inspection, it still remained inconsistent and people were not always supported in an environment that was clean or safeguarded them from the risk of infection. Kitchen surfaces such as cupboards and worktops were sticky to the touch, as were surfaces in certain people’s bedrooms. Some people had cobwebs and dust in their rooms indicating further work was needed to implement the improved standard of cleanliness throughout all parts of the building. However, staff worked alongside people to support them in manage their own personal hygiene to reduce the risk of infections. There was clear guidance in place of how this could be supported for each person, and people were supported to take pride in their appearance.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Involving people to manage risks

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always work well with people to understand and manage risks. Staff did not always provide care to meet people’s needs that was safe, supportive and enabled people to do the things that mattered to them.

Risks to people were not always managed safely or effectively. The people living at the service had diagnosis of complex mental health conditions. Although people’s emotional needs were largely stable, there was a continued lack of clear guidance on how staff should respond in a person-centred way if they were to become anxious or distressed to ensure their wellbeing and safety. For example, signs that a person might be struggling with their emotions were recorded but not how staff should respond if they were to observe these signs.

However, risks posed to people’s physical health were more consistently managed, for example around management of diabetes and risks posed to people with reduced mobility. There was clearer guidance and monitoring in these areas to ensure people’s safety.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning culture

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider had a proactive and positive culture of safety, based on openness and honesty. Staff listened to concerns about safety and investigated and reported safety events. Lessons were learnt to continually identify and embed good practice.

Incidents at The Chestnuts were infrequent, however when they happened, they were investigated and reported appropriately. An investigation was undertaken to identify any contributory factors and learning that could be taken. We saw this was shared with staff, who had an up-to-date knowledge of how people should be supported safely in line with their current needs.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Medicines optimisation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not make sure that medicines and treatments were safe and met people’s needs, capacities and preferences.

Medication management systems were not effective at ensuring people would receive the medication they needed, when they needed it. The service was using multi-compartment compliance aids (MCA’s) in the form of blister bags for all people. These are not recommended by National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) due to the increased risk of medication errors, and that medication does not come with crucial safety information such as side effects. This meant we could not be assured staff would have this information available to refer to. During our inspection we identified some concerns about the temperature medications were being stored at meaning they would be less effective. This had been identified at our previous inspection and remained a concern.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe and effective staffing

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider made sure there were enough qualified, skilled and experienced staff, who received effective support, supervision and development. They worked together well to provide safe care that met people’s individual needs.

There were sufficient staff to support people’s needs safely, who were generally knowledgeable about each person and the care they received. There were robust recruitment systems in place to ensure all staff were suitable to work at The Chestnuts. This included the use of Disclosure and Barring Service (DBS) checks, which are checks against the police national computer to help providers make safer recruitment decisions. Staff received regular supervisions to monitor their knowledge, abilities and welfare. Where more complex tasks were performed such as administering medications, staff had their competency assessed to ensure they were able to do so safely.

There were a small minority of staff who had not completed specific training around mental health. However we found in all other areas, staff had training that reflected the needs of the people they supported. Staff we spoke with could describe how they would support the physical and mental needs of people in their care.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe environments

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always detect and control potential risks in the care environment. They did not always make sure equipment, facilities and technology supported the delivery of safe care.

We identified evidence of people smoking with the building which was not being adequately controlled. The homes most recent independent fire risk assessment stated that people did not smoke within the building, which we identified was not accurate. Although there were controls agreed with people on access to cigarettes, these were not providing effective as it was still happening. There was an outdoor smoking area however this was located outside people’s bedroom windows, which did not reflect consideration to impact this might have on people in these rooms.

The environment was generally in a good state of maintenance, with regular checks taking place around utilities such as electricity, water, gas and fire safety. There were some remaining hazards such as a bathroom where the light was not functioning, and an unlocked boiler cupboard which was very hot to the touch. These were addressed following the inspection.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe systems, pathways and transitions

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider worked with people and healthcare partners to establish and maintain safe systems of care, in which safety was managed or monitored. They made sure there was continuity of care, including when people moved between different services.

There was appropriate guidance and monitoring in place to support people with their complex health needs, and we saw that referrals were made in a timely way when people’s health and wellbeing changed. For example, we saw staff had identified concerns about one person losing weight and had made a referral to the dietician. They were prescribed supplements and regular snacks as a result and had now returned to a stable and healthy weight.

There were systems in place to assess the needs of any people moving into the service to ensure they could be safely met; however nobody had moved into The Chestnuts since our previous inspection.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Safeguarding

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider worked with people and healthcare partners to understand what being safe meant to them and the best way to achieve that. Staff concentrated on improving people’s lives while protecting their right to live in safety, free from bullying, harassment, abuse, discrimination, avoidable harm and neglect. The provider shared concerns quickly and appropriately.

Staff were knowledgeable about their responsibilities to safeguard those in their care from the risk of abuse and neglect. They could confidently describe what signs of concern they may look out for, and what they would do if they were worried that a person was at risk of harm. One staff member told us “I would look out for any bruises, evidence of money being stolen, note changes in behaviour such as people not eating. I would report to my manager and take action to remove the person from danger if needed. If appropriate I could also speak to the local authority, police or CQC to share my concerns”. There had been no safeguarding incidents recently which required reporting to the local authority. People felt safe and one person told us “Yes, I do feel safe. The staff are kind and treat me well”.

People can only be deprived of their liberty to receive care and treatment when this is in their best interests and legally authorised under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 (MCA). In care homes, and some hospitals, this is usually through MCA application procedures called the Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards (DoLS). We checked whether the service was working within the principles of the MCA, whether appropriate legal authorisations were in place when needed to deprive a person of their liberty, and whether any conditions relating to those authorisations were being met. Where the risks to people were deemed sufficient that restrictions such as living in locked accommodation were needed, to ensure their safety, appropriate authorisations were sought and recorded.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Well-led
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Well-led – this means we looked for evidence that service leadership, management and governance assured high-quality, person-centred care; supported learning and innovation; and promoted an open, fair culture.

At our last assessment we rated this key question Inadequate. At this assessment the rating has changed to Requires Improvement. This meant the management and leadership was inconsistent. Leaders and the culture they created did not always support the delivery of high-quality, person-centred care.

The service was in breach of legal regulation in relation to good governance.
keyQuestionRatings.narrative: This service is not always well-led

topicareas.name: Capable, compassionate and inclusive leaders

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Leaders did not understand context in which the provider delivered care, treatment and support. They did not embody the culture and values of their workforce and organisation. Leaders did not have the skills, knowledge, experience and credibility to lead effectively.

Although people and partners we spoke to had noted some improvements had been made by the manager, they did not have a clear vision for the service or knowledge of the people being supported. They had a limited understanding and focus on how people’s mental welfare could be promoted holistically through choice, independence and meaningful activity. We identified that a number of areas continued to fall below the standards expected or reflect best practice care for individuals living with a mental health diagnosis. The manager was not knowledgeable about the people being supported, and when asked to tell us about people stated they had only been at the service for 6 months so did not know people well. Some elements of care such as around activities, food and daily living tasks remained institutionalised and did not consider how people could be challenged to take positive risks.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Freedom to speak up

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider developed a culture where people could speak up and their voice would be heard. However, we could not always see this had happened in practice.

Staff felt comfortable about being able to raise concerns openly, and these would be listened to and acted upon. One staff member told us “I can definitely can speak to my manager or senior carer. They are very open”. Another staff member echoed this and told us “I like the manager. She is very approachable”. Despite this, we identified that people continued to live lives that did not reflect their diverse needs, interests or aspirations. They were not consistently treated with dignity or supported to gain in independence, grow and develop in skills and wellbeing. There was no evidence that this had been identified, and there remained a culture that did not focus on the people in their care.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Governance, management and sustainability

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not have clear responsibilities, roles, systems of accountability or good governance. They did not act on the best information about risk, performance and outcomes, or share this securely with others when appropriate.

There was a regular schedule of audits and checks to ensure the ongoing quality of care, however these were not as effective as they needed to be. They did not consistently ensure the safety of the building, level of cleanliness, accuracy of care documentation or that a clear plan was in place for how people could be supported to achieve their goals and aspirations. Spot checks by provider representatives were undertaken in addition to those completed by the manager, and although they were identifying areas for improvement these had not all been realised at the inspection. For individuals with a learning disability and autistic people, the provider had not fully considered the principles of RSRCRC to ensure they receive care that was person-centred and promoted independence.

There was a business continuity policy to cover any emergencies such as the loss of an important utility or extreme weather event to ensure people would have continuity of care. There was also an on-call system where there was always a management representative available to respond in urgent situations.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning, improvement and innovation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always focus on continuous learning, innovation and improvement across the organisation and local system. They did not always encourage creative ways of delivering equality of experience, outcome and quality of life for people.

Although areas of care delivery had improved since the inspection, it had not yet reached the standard that we would expect. There had been additional training for staff around mental health and a consultant had worked with the service to review care planning documents, but the care being delivered still did not reflect a holistic model that considered all factors that could promote people’s emotional wellbeing.

There were very few incidents recorded at the service, however that that we saw were investigated well and appropriate action taken. This learning was shared within staff meetings, handovers and individual supervisions.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Partnerships and communities

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider understood their duty to collaborate and work in partnership, so services worked seamlessly for people. They shared information and learning with partners and collaborated for improvement.

The service worked closely with partners in their local community to support the needs of people, which included supporting regular appointments with health services for routine checkup’s and if staff were concerned about people’s welfare. Health and care professionals who shared feedback with us spoke of positive relationships with the home. One stakeholder told us “I have a good relationship with the staff and management. They always make me feel welcome”. The provider also worked to form relationships with wider community groups, including mental health support groups which were attended by people regularly, as well as local places of worship.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Shared direction and culture

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not have a clear shared vision, strategy and culture which was based on transparency, equity, equality and human rights, diversity and inclusion, and engagement. They did not understand the challenges and the needs of people and their communities.

There was no clear vision both for the service as a whole, and for what individual people wanted to achieve from living at the service. Although staff and leaders were kind, they had no holistic plan for each person around aspirations or goals and how they could be achieved. People generally participated in activities together and there was a lack of exploration of individual cultures, wishes and preferences. Tasks were generally done on behalf of people with limited evidence of independence and choice being encouraged, or of a clear focus on enabling people to have the best possible quality of life.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Workforce equality, diversity and inclusion

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider valued diversity in their workforce. They worked towards an inclusive and fair culture by improving equality and equity for people who worked for them.

The provider and leaders ensured that staff were treated equally at the work place, and considered how barriers faced by the diverse workforce could be overcome to improve their experience at work. Where people needed to work flexibly around personal commitments such as children, family or any health needs this was supported. One staff member had recently been unwell for a period of time, and spoke highly of the support and care they received from their manager and colleagues. They stated “I got great support from my colleagues and manager. They all rallied round me, and even arranged a video call with the people who I care for which was a nice touched as they were worried having not seen me. It’s a lovely place to work”.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

name: Silverjen Limited
onspdIcbName: NHS Surrey and Sussex Integrated Care Board

regulatedActivities.name: Personal care

inspectionCategories.name: Community based adult social care services

asgRatings.title: Ongoing Assessment for Silverjen Limited - Archived
asgRatings.name: Homecare
asgRatings.commentary:
Date of assessment: 5 August – 27 September 2025

Silverjen Limited is a homecare agency registered to provide personal care to people in their homes. The service is registered to support people living with dementia, eating disorders, mental health conditions, physical disabilities, sensory impairments, substance misuse problems and people with a learning disability and/or autistic people. CQC only inspects where people receive personal care. This helps with tasks related to personal hygiene and eating. Where they do, we also consider any wider social care provided. At the time of the assessment, 91 people were receiving personal care. As part of this assessment, we spoke with 10 people who used the service and 8 relatives.

As the service is registered to provide care to people with a learning disability and/or autistic people, we assessed the service against ‘Right support, right care, right culture’ (RSRCRC) guidance to make judgements about whether the provider guaranteed people with a learning disability and autistic people respect, equality, dignity, choices, independence and good access to local communities that most people take for granted. During this latest assessment, we found the service was able to demonstrate how it was meeting the underpinning principles of RSRCRC in the areas we reviewed.

We conducted this assessment to follow up on the breaches identified during the last inspection and to address information received from the local authority. The last inspection of the service identified breaches in relation to good governance, fit and proper persons employed, and the need for consent (report published 30 September 2022). At this assessment, we found that the provider was no longer in breach of regulations; however, there were still areas for improvement. We have reported on these in the safe and well-led sections of this focused assessment.

Staff were recruited safely and received training relevant to their roles, including in relation to supporting people with a learning disability and/or autistic people. However, there were areas of improvement in relation to staff supervision.

The governance system generally identified shortfalls; however, further improvement was needed to ensure it consistently picked up missing information in care records. While most of the care plans we reviewed were detailed, person-centred and provided clear guidance for staff, we found that 3 people’s care records were not always accurate. The provider acknowledged this and took immediate action, sending us updated records. However, there were missed opportunities to identify and address these issues sooner, as the governance systems had been slow to respond. The impact on people was minimal because managers and staff knew individuals well and took the time to understand their needs.
asgRatings.narrative: The service is not performing as well as it should and we have told the service how it must improve.
asgRatings.overallPeopleExperience:
People and their relatives told us they felt safe when staff supported them and that staff worked well with external partners to ensure a safe transition between services. Staff had completed safeguarding training and knew how to recognise concerns and report these appropriately.

People and their relatives were involved in assessing risks. However, 3 people’s risk assessments contained information which was not always reflective of the current situation. This was an area that needed to improve. However, feedback from people, staff, relatives and healthcare professionals, confirmed that the impact was minimal, as staff knew the individuals well.

People told us staff maintained a safe environment and used appropriate personal protective equipment. However, in 1 person’s care records did not always highlight whether the person understood the risks of potential fires in their home. We saw the provider had worked with the local fire service but had not always recorded additional information such as the person’s understanding of the risk.

People’s medicines were managed safely; however, improvements were needed to ensure all PRN (‘when required’) medicine protocols included the necessary information to help staff recognise the specific symptoms each person may display.

Staff worked with external healthcare professionals and other partners to ensure people received evidence-based care and treatment. People told us staff helped them monitor their health and wellbeing, and worked well with others to achieve positive outcomes. People told us that staff sought consent appropriately before supporting them.

People told us they felt able to approach staff and managers, and that concerns they raised would be addressed. However, improvements were needed to ensure a coherent shared vision across the service, and to make certain that sufficient staff were in place before accepting a new service user so that staff could consistently arrive on time.

keyQuestionRatings.name: Effective
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Effective – this means we looked for evidence that people’s care, treatment and support achieved good outcomes and promoted a good quality of life, based on best available evidence.

At our last assessment we rated this key question requires improvement. At this assessment the rating has changed to good. This meant people’s outcomes were consistently good, and people’s feedback confirmed this.

topicareas.name: Assessing needs

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider made sure people’s care and treatment was effective by assessing and reviewing their health, care, wellbeing and communication needs with them.

Staff completed assessments prior to providing care to a new person. Assessments included information on people’s needs, preferences and communication methods. People and their relatives told us they were involved in the assessment process, and the provider worked with other health and social care providers to ensure they had the information required prior to visiting the person for the first time. One relative told us, “We agreed the support when Silverjen started his care.” A member of staff described how they worked with stakeholders to find the information they needed about a person who was unable to take part in the pre-admission process, “If there’s no capacity, the pre-admission assessment is done with the family or the next of kin, GP and social services, we refer to everyone.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Consent to care and treatment

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider told people about their rights around consent and respected these when delivering person-centred care and treatment.

People and their relatives told us that staff sought consent prior to supporting them and were respectful of their choices. One person told us, “I would say that they are very good at asking my consent before doing something.” We saw there was evidence recorded in relation to people’s lasting power of attorney arrangements and of who was involved in decisions about their care.

Staff had received training to apply the Mental Capacity Act 2005 (MCA) and understood their responsibilities. One member of staff told us, “[MCA is] designed to protect and empower people who may lack capacity about their own decisions about their care treatment. We are always encouraged by the office to ask for consent from the person. You have to ask for everything, from personal care, food choices, everything else.” Another member of staff described the legislation, “Do not assume that someone doesn’t have capacity unless if it’s known. It has to be less restrictive and work in their best interest. Best interest decision [involves] the family, the doctors.”

The registered manager understood their responsibility in ensuring up to date information was available in relation to people’s decision-making. The registered manager told us, “[Previously] we would just ask them in an assessment. We were not asking for the evidence. Now we understand it’s important that we have the documents.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Delivering evidence-based care and treatment

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider planned and delivered care and treatment to people, taking into account what was important and mattered to them. They did this in line with legislation and current evidence-based good practice and standards.

Staff completed assessments in line with national guidance, such as those related to skin integrity and the principles of Right Support, Right Care, Right Culture. Staff had received training to support people with a learning disability and/or autistic people in line with national guidance and understood how to support people effectively. One member of staff said, “They do involve the family and the staff. The care plan is done with the consideration with the patient. It’s person-centred. We make sure that the care plan is centred on the client.” A relative told us, “The carers are competent and show empathy to [person]. They know how to communicate with her. She can moan when she is being washed, but they are very careful with her.”

People told us that staff supported them in choosing their diet and encouraged them to follow a nutritionally balanced one. One person told us, “The carers make my food. I try and vary what I have. Quite a few of them know how to use the air fryer, if they don’t, usually the carer with them can show them.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: How staff, teams and services work together

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider worked well across teams and services to support people. They made sure people only needed to tell their story once by sharing their assessment of needs when people moved between different services.

People had individual hospital passports which detailed, using a traffic light system, what was important to them. This included important information in the event of an emergency or when the person attended appointments, such as healthcare conditions, a list of medicines, communication needs, and likes and dislikes, which could present as triggers for their anxiety.

Staff told us they worked well together and with healthcare professionals. One member of staff said, “Since I’ve worked for them, I’ve never had a hiccup. If you mention something to the office, they straightaway act on it.”

A professional who regularly worked with the service told us staff worked well together with them to achieve positive outcomes for people, “They (staff) contributed meaningfully to assessments, even in cases where it was difficult to establish baseline needs, and their input helped shape appropriate care planning.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Monitoring and improving outcomes

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider routinely monitored people’s care and treatment to continuously improve it. They ensured that outcomes were positive and consistent, and that they met both clinical expectations and the expectations of people themselves. One person told us, “The carers can see that I am in pain and are aware of what I can and can’t do. When I use the stairlift, they make sure I have my seatbelt on.” A relative told us, “I think [manager] from Silverjen keeps in touch with the GP. She orders any creams for [person]. I think the carer would get in touch with [manager] if there was a problem, and then [manager] would let us know.”

Staff understood how to monitor and improve people’s outcomes and care records included information such as the signs to look out for in relation to physical and emotional changes, and what staff should do to monitor and escalate this appropriately. They were supported by the management team whom they could call if they had any questions relating to long-term monitoring and they knew how to escalate urgent concerns. One member of staff told us in relation to monitoring a person’s blood sugar before they leave the person’s home, “You check this before you go. We talk to the managers in the office and document it. 999 if it’s more serious or 111.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Supporting people to live healthier lives

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider supported people to manage their health and wellbeing to maximise their independence, choice and control. Staff supported people to live healthier lives and where possible, reduce their future needs for care and support.

There was clear information recorded on the healthcare professionals involved in people’s care and care records included information on how to effectively support people’s health and wellbeing. One relative told us, “The carers put moisturising cream on [person’s] body. The GP surgery complimented the carers on [person’s] skin care.” Staff told us they understood the importance of ensuring people were supported with their health and psychological wellbeing. One member of staff told us, “I try to be with [person] most of the time and I try to do activities with [person]. I try to cook and we eat together. I give [person] personal care. I try to do most of the things [person] loves to do.”

Care records included information on how to support people with their mouth hygiene and when to refer to the dentist. A member of staff described the information contained in care plans and the steps they would take in relation to mouth hygiene, “[The care plan] says whether they are wearing dentures or their own teeth and if there’s a particular client we should mention what to do with the teeth or if they have dental pain or they need particular cleaners, natural teeth, tongue, gums, lips. All mentioned in the care plans and risk assessments.”

keyQuestionRatings.name: Safe
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Safe – this means we looked for evidence that people were protected from abuse and avoidable harm.

At our last assessment we rated this key question requires improvement. At this assessment the rating has remained requires improvement. This meant some aspects of the service were not always safe and there was limited assurance about safety. There was an increased risk that people could be harmed.
keyQuestionRatings.narrative: This service is not always safe

topicareas.name: Infection prevention and control

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider assessed and managed the risk of infection. They detected and controlled the risk of it spreading and shared concerns with appropriate agencies promptly.

People and their relatives told us staff followed good infection prevention and control (IPC) practices. One person told us, “The carers wear gloves and aprons when doing my personal care.” Another person said, “The carer wears gloves and an apron when they wash and dress me. The carer always looks neat and tidy.”

Staff received regular training in relation to IPC and told us they always had access to sufficient personal protective equipment. There was an infection control policy in place and unannounced spot checks of staff included ensuring they followed appropriate IPC procedures.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Involving people to manage risks

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider generally worked with people to understand and manage risks by thinking holistically. Staff provided care to meet people’s needs that was safe, supportive and enabled people to do the things that mattered to them. However, we identified that 3 people’s risk assessments contained information which was inconsistent. When we made the provider aware, they sent us an updated copy which showed that the areas had been addressed. All other risk assessments we reviewed were detailed, person-centred and contained people’s views. Risk assessments included relevant information including what triggered a person to become anxious, how to manage the risk of falls and how to reduce the risk of developing pressure areas.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning culture

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider had a proactive and positive culture of safety, based on openness and honesty. Staff listened to concerns about safety, and investigated and reported safety events. However, there were potentially missed opportunities to continually identify and embed good practice.

Staff recorded incidents and accidents and generally looked at ways to reduce the risk of these happening again. The provider completed action plans and involved professionals to look at lessons which could be learnt. However, there were instances where the provider potentially missed opportunities when people had complained about carers being late. For example, where newly started care visits had been delayed, the provider did not always ensure they learnt lessons from previous instances of when this had happened to ensure the travelling distance for staff was always manageable. The provider took immediate action when they were made aware by people and the impact was minimal based on the feedback we received from people, relatives and staff. The provider recognised in an open and honest way that there had been potentially missed opportunities. They had already identified this prior to our assessment and had an action plan to address this with an external consultant.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Medicines optimisation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider generally made sure that medicines and treatments were safe and met people’s needs, capacities and preferences. However, there were some areas which could be improved to ensure staff always have the necessary information in relation to people’s PRN (‘when required’) medicines.

Some protocols for ‘when required’ medicines could be further improved. Whilst they generally contained relevant information in line with national guidance, such as the possible side effects, maximum doses and minimum time between doses, these did not always include specific information on how the signs and symptoms may present in that person. The impact on people was minimal based on the feedback we received from people, their relatives and staff. When we informed the provider, they told us they would address this.

People and their relatives told us staff provided the level of support they requested in relation to medicines management. Where people chose to take their medicines independently, staff supported them by undertaking tasks such as collecting medicines from the local pharmacy, so people could continue to take their medicines by themselves. One person told us, “My medicines are in a blister pack which they get out for me.”

The provider had a medicines policy in place and undertook audits of people’s medicine records. Staff had received training to administer medicines and regularly received competency checks. One member of staff told us, “Normally the senior may visit you when you are with your client and they watch you giving the medication and recording it in the [medicine administration] charts.” Where the service was responsible for managing people’s medicines, staff ensured they recorded when they administered these, and there was information in the records in relation to how people took their medicines and the possible side effects.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe and effective staffing

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider made sure there were enough qualified, skilled and experienced staff. They worked together well to provide safe care that met people’s individual needs. However, we identified areas for improvement in relation to some staff training and staff supervision.

People and their relatives told us staff had not missed any visits and were generally on time. When staff were late, the provider took action to address this. There was a system of informing people when staff were running late, and staff told us they had enough time to travel between care visits. One person who used the service told us, “They usually ring me up if the bus is not on time, and they are running late. I did complain once about a carer that was always late, but they sorted it out and I got a new carer.” Staff told us they had sufficient time to travel between visits and received support if they required further time to travel. A member of staff told us, “I do those antisocial hours. I feel if I need support, I get support. If I need to swap my shift with someone, I get support.”

Staff were recruited safely to the service. This included requesting and receiving references from previous employers, employment histories with gaps explained, right-to-work documentation and Disclosure and Barring Service (DBS) checks. DBS checks are carried out to confirm whether prospective new staff had a criminal record or were barred from working with people at the time.

Whilst staff received supervisions according to the provider’s policy, previous supervision action points were not always followed up consistently, and supervisions were mostly carried out remotely. When we informed the provider, they stated that they had already identified and addressed this issue going forward. Staff told us supervisions took place regularly and they were able to discuss areas such as people’s needs, training and workload. One member of staff told us, “We talk about the flexibility of the rota, whether you are happy with it or if you need some changes, time management.”
Staff received unannounced spot checks undertaken by the management team to ensure they were following the correct procedures, arrived on time and provide support to staff. One member of staff told us, “Sometimes we just get there and they (management) come [unannounced]. They will check the manual handling. They observe you and look at you. If they have concerns, they will guide you."

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe environments

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider generally detected and controlled potential risks in the care environment. They made sure equipment, facilities and technology supported the delivery of safe care. We saw there was guidance for staff on how to ensure the premises they visited were safe whilst respecting people’s homes. People and their relatives told us they felt staff knew how to maintain a safe environment and how to use equipment. One person told us, “The carers are competent in using the hoist. It is serviced every year.” Staff had referred concerns related to the environment to the relevant parties and ensured these were addressed promptly. For example, in one instance staff noted that the light fitting had fallen from the ceiling in a person’s home, and they worked with the housing association to arrange for a qualified person to rectify this on the same day.

However, in one instance we found that a person had been prescribed a flammable cream. Although staff had worked with the fire service, who provided guidance to reduce the risk of fire, there were additional areas the provider could have assessed, for example, clearly recording that the person understood the associated risks. Following our site visit, the provider shared an updated version of the person’s care records.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe systems, pathways and transitions

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider worked with people and healthcare partners to establish and maintain safe systems of care, in which safety was managed or monitored. They made sure there was continuity of care, including when people moved between different services.

People and their relatives described how the provider worked with other organisations, such as physiotherapists and the local authority, to ensure the transition to the service and to other services was safe. One person told us how staff worked with partners to ensure their alarm pendant to summon for help worked effectively when they were on their own, “I have an alarm which I can put around my neck if I am on my own. The carers use the key box for entry.” The provider explained how they ensured oversight when people transitioned between services, for example by working with the hospital discharge team and the person’s family doctor.

Care records included information that helped ensure people could move easily between services. The provider had a business continuity plan, and this explained how staff should prioritise care in the event of different emergencies.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Safeguarding

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider worked with people and healthcare partners to understand what being safe meant to them and the best way to achieve that. Staff concentrated on improving people’s lives while protecting their right to live in safety, free from bullying, harassment, abuse, discrimination, avoidable harm and neglect. The provider shared concerns quickly and appropriately.

People and their relatives told us they felt safe with staff. One person told us, “I feel safe when they are in the house.” A relative told us, “I think they respect [person] and treat her well. They always make sure she is okay before they leave.”

The provider had a safeguarding policy in place, and staff knew how to recognise signs of abuse and report these internally and externally. One member of staff told us, “You have to document and record in your notes, do the body map, match it, report it to the office [and] safeguarding.” Another member of staff said, “If the person can’t tell you, you could see it from their face, or bruising. Of course [you can tell] the office. You’d have to whistleblow [and] you have the safeguarding team.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Well-led
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Well-led – this means we looked for evidence that service leadership, management and governance assured high-quality, person-centred care; supported learning and innovation; and promoted an open, fair culture.

At our last assessment we rated this key question requires improvement. At this assessment the rating has remained requires improvement. This meant the management and leadership was inconsistent. Leaders and the culture they created did not always support the delivery of high-quality, person-centred care.
keyQuestionRatings.narrative: This service is not always well-led

topicareas.name: Capable, compassionate and inclusive leaders

evidenceCategory.commentary: Not all leaders understood the context in which the provider delivered care, treatment and support. The registered manager acknowledged that, while significant improvements had been made to the service, further work was still needed. As part of their action plan, they were in the process of recruiting an external consultant to help them embed the improvements effectively and consistently. One relative told us, “Generally, I would say Silverjen are very good, however I have requested a list of which carers are coming, prior to visits, but for no particular reason, they don’t seem able to provide this.” Staff told us they felt leaders valued them and were supportive. One member of staff told us, “Yes, I feel supported. I would go straight to my manager if a problem is not solved. I am all satisfied.” Another member of staff told us, “I feel supported by them (management). We have enough time.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Freedom to speak up

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider fostered a positive culture where people felt they could speak up and their voice would be heard.

Staff told us they felt able to speak up if they had concerns. One member of staff said, “If there’s any concerns, the management will tell us and we work how to improve. They always support. They listen to suggestions. They ask for input from carers.” Another member of staff said in relation to speaking up, “I can certainly. It’s always acted upon.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Governance, management and sustainability

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always have clear responsibilities, roles, systems of accountability or good governance.

There were governance systems in place which ensured the quality of the service was monitored. However, these were not always effective in identifying shortfalls we found in relation to 3 people’s care records. However, this had minimal impact on people as staff knew their needs well and the provider was open and honest about the areas they felt they needed to improve. Audits of other areas, such as the environment, IPC and medicines management, were effective. The provider had created an action plan, which they were working through at the time of the assessment.

People told us management visited their homes to spot check staff and that they were given the opportunity to provide feedback on the service. One person told us, “I think [manager] does a spot check on the carer from time to time.” Another person commented, “They quite often send me feedback forms. I don’t have any suggestions because all is good with the organisation.”

Staff told us they knew how to perform in their role and where to go if they needed support in their job. A member of staff told us, “We have managers in the office, if we have any concerns then we communicate with them.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning, improvement and innovation

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not always focus on continuous learning, innovation and improvement across the organisation and local system. They did not always encourage creative ways of delivering equality of experience, outcome and quality of life for people. They did not always actively contribute to safe, effective practice and research. Whilst the provider was taking action in response to the shortfalls they and our assessment had identified, progress for some of the areas such as improving care records, had been slow. Additional time was required to fully embed the recently implemented practices. The provider openly acknowledged this during the assessment and stated that they were sourcing an external consultant to help them implement the areas for improvement.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Partnerships and communities

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider understood their duty to collaborate and work in partnership, so services worked seamlessly for people. They shared information and learning with partners and collaborated for improvement.

The provider worked well with partners in the local community. We saw staff had referred relevant information to the local authority, for example when a person required a food voucher. Once the voucher was received, staff worked with local organisations and ensured they collected the groceries so that the person was able to have a meal.

Partners who worked with the service told us they felt that staff collaborated with them and took on board feedback from them. One professional told us, “Communication was clear, and there was a strong sense of coordination across the team. It was evident that leadership within the agency fostered a culture of accountability and responsiveness.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Shared direction and culture

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider lacked a clear shared vision, strategy, and culture, which was based on transparency, equity, equality, human rights, diversity, inclusion, and engagement. We found that the provider had made significant improvements since the last inspection. However, the provider acknowledged that further work was needed to ensure care records were always accurate, and they had already recognised, prior to this latest assessment, that they needed external help, which they had started the process for. For example, we identified that the culture was one where the provider accepted new people into the service but did not always have the resources available in that particular geographical area when the care package was due to commence. Although we observed that the provider consistently addressed these issues, and people reported that the impact had been minimal, it revealed further areas for improvement, particularly in relation to all staff having a shared direction. One person told us in relation to the culture, “Silverjen seem to be a good organisation. My only grumble would be that the carers seem to cover a large area. I think it would be better if they just covered one area. They always apologise if they are late, which seems to be because they travel such long distances.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Workforce equality, diversity and inclusion

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider valued diversity in their workforce. They worked towards an inclusive and fair culture by improving equality and equity for people who worked for them.

Staff had completed training on equality, diversity, and inclusion, as well as the importance of respecting each other’s differences. Staff undertook shadowing sessions with a more senior colleague and received most of their training face-to-face. The registered manager told us they encouraged good teamwork and wanted everyone to feel included. One member of staff told us in relation to equality, diversity and inclusion training, “They are checking that we have done it. We do a lot of training.” Another member of staff said, “There should not be any discrimination between clients and staff and staff and staff in case of gender, ethnicity, age, everyone should be treated equally. Some clients have disabilities and there should not be any discrimination.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

asgRatings.title: Ongoing Assessment for Silverjen Limited
asgRatings.name: Homecare
asgRatings.commentary:
Date of assessment: 5 and 10 August 2026.

Silverjen Limited is a domiciliary care agency providing personal care and support to people in their own homes. Silverjen Limited supports people with complex health and care needs. There were 66 people being supported with personal care at the time of our assessment.

The inspection was prompted by concerns raised relating to safe care and treatment and staffing levels: we conducted a focused inspection of the key questions Safe and Well-Led to assess these risks. The location was previously rated Requires Improvement in December 2025. This has now changed to Inadequate following our inspection. We identified 4 breaches of legal regulation in relation to safe care and treatment, safeguarding people from abuse and neglect, good governance and safe staffing.

We found people were receiving unsafe care, which placed them at greater risk of harm or deteriorating health: risks were poorly managed with people having complex health or care needs that staff were unaware of. There was a lack of detailed records about people’s health and care needs, and an absence of guidance to inform staff how to provide care safely.

There were insufficient staff to ensure people had their needs met safely: we found multiple instances of significantly delayed calls, and multiple instances of staff not staying for the amount of time they should: this impacted people’s safety. There was a poor level of staff training and competence: staff training had not been prioritised by the provider, and staff supported people without having the right skills or knowledge to do so.

Leadership was inadequate: the provider and registered manager had limited understanding of the needs of people being supported and had not identified the serious and widespread risks identified at this inspection. Governance and quality monitoring of people’s care, undertaken by the provider were poor: when areas of improvements had been identified by them or their staff, they had not taken action or ensured sufficient improvements were made.

Documentation on how staff should support people was inadequate, and records of care did not clearly evidence how people were being supported in a way that met their needs or reflected best practices, including management of medicines and incidents. We found that medications had been administered in an unsafe way by staff who were not sufficiently knowledgeable on how to do so and there was inadequate guidance in place to ensure people were only receiving medication when they needed to.

People could not be assured they would be safe from harm or abuse. When the provider identified that people were at risk of harm from staff or from incidents, they had not taken action to protect people, and this meant people remained at ongoing risk of abuse. Incidents were not consistently learned from, and safeguarding incidents were not always appropriately reported in line with the providers legal responsibilities.

We assessed the service against ‘Right support, right care, right culture’ guidance to make judgements about whether the provider guaranteed autistic people and people with a learning disability respect, equality, dignity, choices, independence and good access to local communities that most people take for granted. The service was not reflecting this guidance, and people were not treated with respect or as individuals.

In instances where CQC has begun a process of regulatory action, we may publish this information on our website after any representations and/or appeals have been concluded, if the action has been taken forward. This service has been placed in special measures. The purpose of special measures is to ensure that services providing inadequate care make significant improvements. Special measures provide a framework within which we use our enforcement powers in response to inadequate care and provide a time frame within which providers must improve the quality of the care they provide.
asgRatings.narrative: The service is performing badly and we've taken action against the person or organisation that runs it.
asgRatings.overallPeopleExperience:
People’s feedback on their experiences of care was varied. Several people and relatives said they did not always feel [people were] safe or listened to.

People’s overall experiences were affected by the deployment of staff, staffing levels and poor rota planning. The lateness of calls and staff not always staying for the full length of the calls impacted the care people received. This included a delay in being supported with meals, drinks, re-positioning and receiving their medicines.

People fed back there was a lack of communication from the office and they felt the leadership needed to be strengthened.

However, there were people that felt they received safe care. There were also relatives that fed back people were well looked after and that their loved ones had good relationships with staff.
